               <ns0:head>CHAP. XXIV.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p>ANd <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">From the time that <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was come to <ns0:hi>Cesarea,</ns0:hi> the malice and fury of the persecutors was very great, stick not at any travel and pains to do mischief with; and surely we ought to be as earnest in doing good, or their zeal will condem us.</ns0:note> after five days, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 23.2.</ns0:note> Ananias the high priest descended with the elders, and <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> a certain <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A Lawyer to form the Indictment against <ns0:hi>Paul,</ns0:hi> or to aggravate his fault, and to desire Judgment up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on him. Such Advocates usually were the chiefest Orators, as <ns0:hi>Demosthenes</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Greece,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Cicero</ns0:hi> at <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi>; and <ns0:hi>Tertul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lus</ns0:hi> seems to have been his Crafts-master, whom the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> hired</ns0:note> oratour <ns0:hi>named</ns0:hi> Tertullus who <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">to draw up an accusation against <ns0:hi>Paul.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> enform<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed the governour against Paul.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">When <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was sent for to appear, being under the custody of the Soldiers who brought him to <ns0:hi>Cesaria.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> when he was called forth, Tertullus began to accuse <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> saying, <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">It being one of the rules of Art, which an Orator seldom forgets, to endeavour to obtain the Judges favour, <ns0:hi>Tertullus</ns0:hi> commends <ns0:hi>Felix,</ns0:hi> who indeed had delivered that Country from some Robbers (like Banditi, or Moss-Troopers) that did infest it; but is commended for little else amongst the Historians, who brand him for extraordinary covetousness and cruelty.</ns0:note> Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness, and that very worthy deeds are done unto this nation by thy providence,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">We commend and admire it. It is most certain, that inferiors enjoy many benefits by the means of their Gover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nors, who bear the burthen for the people, watching, and caring for them; and that a bad Government is better than none, and therefore not only <ns0:hi>Tertullus</ns0:hi> (who may well be thought<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to speak out of flattery) but St. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> himself, <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 10. speaks with great respect unto <ns0:hi>Felix.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> We accept <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> always, and in all places, most noble Felix, with all thankfulness.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Notwithstanding, that I be not <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Hinder thee, or take thee away from other occasions; this is another artifice of an Orator, to promise brevity, especially when he speaks to men of employment or busi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:note> farther te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dious unto thee, I pray thee, that thou wouldest hear us of thy clemency a few words.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 For we have found this man <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">A Pest, or Plague, the Abstract being put for the Concrete, as implying, that no word he could use could properly signify the mischievousness of that man,</ns0:note> a pestilent fel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low, and a <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">whom he falsly charges with Sedition (not that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> would have disliked him for that, had it been true; but) to make St. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> the more odious, and in danger of his Life.</ns0:note> mover of sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ring-leader of the <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or Heresie, which in common use was then taken more favou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rably for any Doctrine.</ns0:note> sect of the <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Of the Christian<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>; for they who out of <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi> were called Christians, in <ns0:hi>Iudea</ns0:hi> were called <ns0:hi>Nazarens.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> did call our Saviour and his follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers thus, it being accounted an ignominious term; and they who were born at <ns0:hi>Nazareth</ns0:hi> disgraced by it, as appears by <ns0:hi>Nathaneel</ns0:hi>'s question, <ns0:hi>Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth</ns0:hi>?
